utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we begin, there are one or two administrative matters. First of all, we have looked at the statement of Witness -- what was Witness K28. We will admit that statement under Rule 92 bis, subject to any submissions that are made about it. The other matter is this: Mr. Milosevic, last night I mentioned the witness statement, and I should explain the position to you so that you understand it. Normally the rule, the procedure is that the Judges do not have the original witness statements of the witnesses when they give evidence live, so we haven't got the statement of this witness at the moment. We haven't seen it yet. To explain matters further, we do have the statements if the Prosecution submit the statements under Rule 92 bis, we have those, of course. But for any witness who gives evidence live, we do not have the witness statements unless they are formally exhibited in the case, in which case we have them. And I think it's right that in virtually every case so far, that has happened. Now, if you want us to have this witness's statement, say so and we will get a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. You can certainly have the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have copies, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Prepared and coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecution Exhibit 151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: , Mr. Milosevic, would you bear in mind that both question and answer have to be interpreted, so would you leave a gap after the witness has given his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. By all means. I'll take care about that. I'll turn on the English interpretation. But before I continue, Mr. May, you interrupted me yesterday when I was quoting the statement of his party, Novo Demokratija, from yesterday's newspapers, because you said that you were not interested in comments made by journalists. Now, since I have the official statement, the official press release of Novo Demokratija, a faxed copy of it, it's on their writing paper, you can see it, and we can also have it displayed on the overhead projector, with a seal and a signature of a member of their leadership. It is Mrs. Rebeka Srbinovic who signed this, who was authorised to sign this. I'm going to quote only a few positions so that both you and the public would know what this is all about. So this is Novo Demokratija whose president is the current Minister of the Interior, that is to say my opponent, not my friend. No associate of mine, it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can put any matters in it to the witness for his comments. The statement of that party is not, at the moment evidence, but you can put it to the witness for his comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to put it to the witness right now, just a few quotes from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They claim that at these round-table discussions and these activities, these debates related to Kosovo, the state authorities took part in no way, nor the representatives of the state security services both home and abroad. That is the first fact. I'm going to present a few facts and then he can make a comment. The second fact is related to Ratomir Tanic, a founder of WIDI [phoen], of the reformists, and Vice-President of the Civil Alliance of Serbia. It says here in this statement: "Who from that position became a sympathiser of Novo Demokratija" And then she speaks of these public activities, the organisation of meetings, et cetera. "Outside these public activities, there were no plans on the resolution of the Kosovo and Metohija problem, nor did anybody -- nor was anybody authorised on behalf of Novo Demokratija to make such plans with anybody, including the persons Mr. Tanic mentions, such as Markovic, Dojcilo Maslovaric, Jovica Stanisic, Momcilo Perisic, Mira Markovic, Slobodan Milosevic, and the representatives of diplomatic missions in our country. No one in Novo Demokratija was aware of the purported contacts that Tanic had with secret services home and abroad. So this is his personal activity, and this has nothing to do with Mr. Tanic's participation in certain international activities organised by Novo Demokratija. Tanic testifies --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pause there. The witness must be given the opportunity to answer what is being said. Now, Mr. -- just a moment. Rather than -- so that the witness has a fair opportunity to answer these allegations which are being made, he must be allowed to do so. Therefore, if it's put in parts which he can deal with, he should be able to answer. Now, let him answer that. You've heard, Mr. Tanic, what's said, what's been said, apparently, by this spokesman, spokeswoman. Have you any comments you wish to make about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I start with my comments? I'll try to be concise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the claim that at round-table discussions and at scientific meetings dedicated to resolving the Kosovo problem, there was no participation by the authorities of the Republic of Serbia and of the SDB. First and foremost, I never said that the SDB took part in round-table discussions devoted to the problem of Kosovo. However, I did say that the representatives of the ruling coalition, of the three parties of the ruling coalition did take part. I don't want to present any kind of general thesis, but I'm just going to mention by way of proof a gathering that was organised in 1994 and 1995 - please don't take my word for it - so in the mid-'90s at any rate. It was organised by the British Ambassador, Ivor Roberts, the British Ambassador in Belgrade. And the ruling parties attended: The SPS, the party of Mr. Milosevic was there, represented by Goran Percevic; and from the JUL party, there was Mr. Vladimir Stambuk and Mrs. Jelica Stambuk as representatives of JUL; Percevic as a representative of the SPS; and then Tahir Hasanovic and I took part as representatives of Novo Demokratija; then Fehmi Agani as a representative of the Albanians or, rather, a representative of Rugova's party. There were also other members from Albanian political life; Surroi, Vllasi, et cetera. And also the representatives of the Diplomatic Corps from Belgrade or, rather, the embassies of all countries of the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down. You're going too fast. And could you deal with it a little more concisely. We have that point. Now, is there any other answer you want to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just mentioned the particular gathering by way of proof, which shows that this claim is not correct. The second assertion, that no one was aware of my contacts with foreign intelligence services -- oh, I'm sorry. The second claim, that no one was aware of my contacts with the security services, first of all, it is quite normal that these contacts are not advertised all over, so it is only natural that all members of the party would not be aware of that. And secondly, I did not have any kind of illegal contacts with any security service, either home or abroad, foreign services or domestic services. As I already said, I had certain contacts related to the intelligence dimension of legal political issues like the Dayton Agreement, like the struggle against terrorism, like the dialogue in Kosovo. Such contacts Mr. Milosevic also had through his authorised representatives, both with the CIA and other intelligence organisations. For example, the head of the CIA, Mr. William Deutsche, paid a public visit to our security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have the point. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But this pertains to only part of it, this point made by Mr. Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please read on. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside these public political frameworks, there were no plans on resolving the Kosmet problem.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I respond to this? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let the question finish. Yes. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "On behalf of Novo Demokratija, no one was authorised to make such plans with anyone, including persons that Mr. Tanic mentions, Ratko Markovic, Dojcilo Maslovaric, Jovica Stanisic, Momcilo Perisic, Mira Markovic, Slobodan Milosevic, and the representatives of diplomatic missions in our country."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This assertion is also incorrect. There is an official document from the meeting of the Executive Committee and the Presidency of Novo Demokratija on several occasions. I'm going to mention only one of them. Before the meeting in New York, a platform was adopted by the Novo Demokratija authorities, that is to say the Executive Committee and the Presidency, and it is exactly the way I described it. That is one thing. Second thing, I never said that any one of us was authorised to make agreements with Mr. Jovica Stanisic, Perisic, Milosevic, or any other persons in relation to Kosovo, rather, the Kosovo problem. I just said that in three and a -- during three and a half years, there was a negotiating process related to Kosovo, that I was one of the participants in this process, that along with me there were other participants as well, and that this political negotiating process was sufficient to prevent the war, that Milosevic supported it, but in 1997 he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no contest that there was this public participation, but is it clear that this participation in round-table discussions and, as we will see later, the participation in these other activities, like of the Bertelsmann Foundation and these meetings of free intellectuals, as you call them, were no negotiations. This was a presentation of use by free intellectuals. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Round-table discussions were the presentation of use by free intellectuals and politicians but I did not say these were only round-table discussions. Apart from that, there were also clear negotiations with a view to preparing an agreement on Kosovo, and authorised representatives of all three parties in the ruling coalition took part in this. I am prepared to present evidence with regard to this and call additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, but they claim the opposite, that there were no plans. I quoted that already, and I don't want to mention it again because it's already part of the transcript. I'm quoting yet again their official paper. The third fact, that: "The content of the testimony of Mr. Tanic testifies to his attempt to construct a story in which Novo Demokratija did not take part in the way he has depicted this, nor did he have such importance as is the one that he wishes to have attached to himself. To the best of our knowledge, Mr. Tanic least of all, least of all could have been a partner to Mr. Milosevic in the building and conduct of some kind of plan for restoring the autonomy to Kosovo and Metohija and resolving the crisis in the province." And then what I read to you yesterday: "Imagination does all sorts of things and sometimes necessity even more than that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. Now, Mr. Tanic, you should have the opportunity to comment on that passage which has been read to you if you wish to. It may be that you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why not? Why would I not wish to? There's nothing there which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't argue. Just answer. If you don't want to comment, don't comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is as follows: First of all, I never claimed that I was a partner in the negotiations with Mr. Milosevic but that he was included in the negotiations as well, and that from time to time, linked to the topics of those negotiations, I had contacts with his closest associates and with him in order to dovetail our positions. I never said we were partners. Had we been partners, I would probably be here as an accused before this Tribunal as well. Now, as far as the statement that my party made, it says in the second part of that statement that they did not know what I did. And in the first part of the statement, they comment on my work, on what I did do. That seems to me be illogical. And third, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment. Try not to comment on what's said. Just answer, please. Is there anything more you want to say about this point? You've made the point that you weren't a partner and you never said you were. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say that perhaps the accused would like to see the contents of two books which bears out the position of Novo Demokratija very similar to the views I am putting forward here today. Or perhaps he doesn't want to see those books. I am not representing the Novo Demokratija party here either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In continuation, the statement says the following: That is to say apart from the public round-table meetings, he did not comment on what I quoted a moment ago, that Novo Demokratija did not take part in the way it did.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I comment? May I comment? I forgot to comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have something more to add. I can't waste time on this because Mr. May is going to curtail my time anyway. Now he goes on to say, does anybody -- "Whether anybody else instrumentalised Mr. Tanic, we cannot know," and so on and so forth. Now, I shall provide you with the entire contents of the statement. It is up to the Tribunal to assess the credibility of Mr. Tanic's statement, testimony, and Novo Demokratija does not wish this to turn into a circus in which witnesses will be witnesses of newspaper articles and facts published in the media. And so on and so forth. So this document has been signed and stamped by the Novo Demokratija seal and person responsible, so you can put this as an attachment to this brilliant witness whom you have brought forth here, and I will continue with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. That is enough, Mr. Milosevic, with that sort of comment. Quite unnecessary. Now, since you've quoted from that document, you should hand it over to the Prosecution. Let the Prosecution have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would also advise, although your defence is entirely a matter for you, that you consider seriously calling this spokesperson as a witness in your case, the spokesperson on behalf of Novo Demokratija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take the document. Give the document to the usher, will you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading -- yes. Yes, please go ahead, take it. You can take it. You can also take a better copy from their website. There's no problem in that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to respond to what was laterally said, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not asked a question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can respond briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Outside that, the president of the Novo Demokratija, Dusan Mihajlovic, with me or alone took part in some of these meetings, and that can be proved very easily through witness statements. I'm not thinking of the round-table meetings but outside that. And I would like to tender two documents which show that I took part in the formulation of the strategic policy of the Novo Demokratija, if the Tribunal would like to have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would wish to exhibit that document, Mr. Milosevic. I'm not sure if it went back to you. It may have done. Yes. If you would hand it over, we'll get it translated and it can be exhibited. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. May I be allowed to ask a question in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know about ask a question. I think you were prevented from making some comment that you wanted to. If you want to say something about that document, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't wish to comment on the document because I want to respect your guidelines not to comment. I should just like to ask the Trial Chamber that if this document is tendered, that the new documents and archive documents be tendered as well which confirm my role in the Novo Demokratija. I have some of them, but there are many more documents in the archives of the party. And also to have this person come in as a witness as well, because he challenges completely and overrides completely what I said, my relevance. So these documents from Novo Demokratija will confirm that I took part in formulating the strategy of the Novo Demokratija with the president himself, the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's no doubt a matter which can be dealt with in re-examination. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's now move on to one of the main points of your statement. First, let me remind you of what you said and then I'll go on and ask you a question. You claim that at a reception in July 1997, in JUL, that I said that at Kosovo there were fewer than 1 million Albanians. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that in anger you said you would show and demonstrate that there were less than a million.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, in the statement it says it the way I said it.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can't say it the way I said it because that's not what I stated. I said that you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, would you both remember --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- to pause. If this matter is to continue, it is to be done so that the interpreters can do their work properly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The point isn't what you seem to be insisting upon now. I'm saying that you claim that in July 1997, in JUL, I said that there were less than a million Albanians. Is that correct? In Kosovo and Metohija, that is.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that you claimed that there were fewer. I said that you would demonstrate and show that there were fewer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What my note says is that you, Mr. Milosevic, replied that he would show there were less than 1 million Albanians or 10 per cent. Therefore, they would not have autonomy. That's what my note has. If there's something in the statement you want to put to the witness, Mr. Milosevic, you can, but that was his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as you said less than 10 per cent a moment ago, did I say that there were less than 10 per cent on that occasion? Is that what you're saying too?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't say that then. This came as an additional explanation but you didn't say that then and I didn't say that in that context. I just gave an explanation as to why below a million. You weren't as precise and specific as that. Far be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you made this as your additional information, is that it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I got this from my conversations with your associates and also with some of your lower -- other statements. But let's move on to the point, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you; you are not questioning me. Therefore, you, of course, claim that you heard this assertion from other personages that you talked as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of that was in the internal communication of the Serbian government and parliament, something along those lines. That was very compatible with those statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah, yes, right. Now we can move on. And for us to be able to move on without any burdens, let's clarify this point. I heard about those assessments and appraisals as well and I considered them to be realistic because several hundred thousand Albanians were outside Kosovo, living abroad, and it was no secret whatsoever -- do you remember that, at least -- it was no secret whatsoever in talks held between various people that in Kosovo there were fewer than a million Kosovo Albanians? So what?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer, respond, and comment, or this -- or is this a comment? May I have your instructions, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. Milosevic for his frankness. I never doubted it. And this is the first time that I saw -- hear that there was a general assessment that there were less than a million of them, that is to say, an official assessment. This is something that I've heard for the first time here today. Usually a figure of 2 or 300.000 more than a million were quoted. It is correct that some of them were abroad. It is correct that they had come over from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of the fact, for example, that this figure was a subject of free comment, both with representatives of the American delegation and foreign delegations and so on and so forth. This was something that was openly commented on, because the question was constantly being asked as to how many Albanians there actually were in Kosovo and Metohija. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the question. It is a legitimate question because the Albanians inflated their numbers up to 2 million. However, I do not know that the official policy was such that it said there were a considerable number less than a million or less than a million at any rate. That is something that I have been informed of for the first time as to its being official policy, so thank you for your honesty and frankness on that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, the assessment of a figure is not official -- of an official position. It is just an assessment of figures, an evaluation of figures. Politics is an activity with a purpose, and an estimation as to how many people there are in this courtroom, for example, is just an endeavour to establish a fact. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let us stop the argument and move on to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that several hundred thousand Albanians at that time were outside Kosovo, living abroad?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. Some were -- left because of their economic state and others because of repression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you of the reasons, I'm just asking whether you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you took that figure of persons who were abroad, would it be so much less than a million, than that figure of a million, if you deduct the number living abroad, in Kosovo at present?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be very difficult. And anyway, those people living abroad also have the right to vote. The fact that they are abroad does not mean that they have left once and for all, for good and that they would have nothing to do with Kosovo. But I'm not an advocate of Kosovo Albanians. We're just dealing with discrepancies in figures and the discrepancy is 2 to 300.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I'm not talking about our conversation because the two of us never discussed -- never discussed anything, never had talks. I'm asking you about the figures that you are presenting, that you are putting forward and for which you claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the argument is pointless at this stage. But what would help us is to know this: Are you saying that this comment was never made by you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying, Mr. May, that I never talked to Mr. Tanic, and I'm not asking -- I'm not answering the questions here but Mr. Tanic is answering the questions. Now, if you're interested in this assertion, this statement, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not moving on. If you're saying that you didn't have this conversation, then you should put it to the witness so he can have the opportunity to answer and deal with it. Just a moment. Let the witness deal with that assertion. What Mr. Tanic has said is that Mr. Milosevic never spoke to you, never spoke in your presence, never said anything about a million Albanians in your presence. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are two assertions. First of all, the assertion that we never spoke. That is incorrect and I can prove otherwise, that we did talk, at least on several occasions. He said he never spoke to me in his life. I say that we spoke several times, and I can bring five to ten witnesses here whom I assume I would have the right to bring in to bear that out. Now, that second assertion that we didn't specifically speak about that figure of under a million, that is also incorrect. But for that second specific conversation, I cannot bring in five to ten witnesses to confirm it as I can for the first assertion to bear out the fact that Mr. Milosevic and I spoke at least on several occasions. So both these assertions are incorrect and I propose that I bring evidence to prove the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the second assertion, all I'm doing is asking Mr. Tanic whether he is aware of the fact that that subject, that topic, that is to say how many Albanians there actually are in Kosovo, was an element which was freely discussed. It was no secret at all. That is the point of what I'm asking you. You didn't learn about any -- learn any secret piece of information. People discussed the fact, that is to say, how many Kosovo Albanians there actually were in Kosovo. This is no discovery. It's not a discovery of any kind. This was freely discussed with foreigners and with our own people. So it was a very ordinary question that was put forward. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness should have the chance to answer these long questions, if they are questions. What is being asserted is that this figure or these kind of discussions were common at the time. Is that right, Mr. Tanic, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Discussions as to the number of Albanians were common, but discussions as to the fact that there were under a million of them were not common.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's make a small digression before we continue along those lines. As you claim that I told you that at a reception in JUL in 1997, where were we standing when we were talking at that reception? Tell me where we were standing, the two of us, or sitting, or whatever you like. Where were we? Describe it.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the JUL building is in Djura Djakovica Street. It is a villa. There is a reception salon looking out onto the garden, onto the yard. On the left-hand side, you go into a separate room which is where Mr. Milosevic, as was his custom, would have dinner after or, rather, towards the end of the reception with his close associates. I was not among those. But we were standing somewhere there between the large salon and the other room that was shut off with a curtain where Mr. Milosevic and his close associates would be having dinner. So that's where we were talking. We talked for a very brief time. I didn't say it was a meeting, we just spoke briefly and then I talked to Mr. Mirko Marjanovic and so on and so forth, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, as receptions in JUL take place every day on the 23rd of July, that means when the days are hottest in summer, and they were held every year in absolutely the same manner, all those thousands of people who attended, including the member -- numerous members of the diplomatic corps, church officials, and so on and so forth will be able to tell you that the receptions in JUL were held --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are asking questions, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I finish? Will be able to tell you -- they will be able to tell you--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... a speech, and now you're making a speech about what you claim the other -- the church officials and others would say. You're here to ask questions. So just ask a question. No, Mr. Tanic, don't you join in. Mr. Milosevic, ask a question. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, therefore, what I said, that thousands of people who were invited to the reception, that receptions in JUL in July were held in the garden? They were garden parties and not held in the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is being put is that the reception was in the garden. Now, is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only that party, all parties, no exception whatsoever. These parties are held on the 23rd of July, and they were invariably garden parties, not indoor parties.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parties are held in the garden and the doors are open and of course there were a great many guests and that's why the garden was open and the building itself. Mr. Milosevic was a gracious host, he tried to talk at least a bit to each and every guest. And as far as politics is concerned, it depended on the subject involved, sometimes it was a friendly conversation, sometimes not exactly. I'm surprised that such general things related to Mr. Milosevic's work are something that he denies now. So the parties were indoors and in the garden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So parties were in the garden. Now let's go back to our question. In mid-July, that is to say at the time of that reception, you know the dates very well and there is no contest about that, this was after the signing of this agreement between Rugova and myself on the subject of education at the time of the implementation of the Dayton Agreement and when tensions were going down, was there an expectation that things would start precisely as you had defined in your statement; that is, the reintegration of Kosovo Albanians in the political life of Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. That was the objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But I mean precisely in that atmosphere, in mid-1997, that is. There was an expectation that was expressed that the process of reintegrating Kosovo Albanians into the political life of Serbia and Yugoslavia would come about. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was already in the spring of 1997, but yes, that's the way it was. I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, do you remember that precisely on that 23rd of July, that is to say the day when this reception was held, in the evening, that on that 23rd of July, 1997, in the morning, in the Assembly of Yugoslavia, I took my oath and took over the office of President of Serbia, precisely on that day? On the 23rd of July, 1997.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember things -- I did not present things that were not part of the Kosovo problem. You don't really have to remind anyone of that oath. I don't know whether this is just a statement or a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is whether you remember that, on that day, I assumed the office of the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On that day, on the 23rd of July, 1997. This is, after all, a public piece of information, and there is no denying that.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, don't go over old matters again. Mr. Tanic, if you remember something, just say yes and no. We'll get on more quickly without your commenting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that a week before that, I had been elected. On the 23rd of July I took over the office, and at a ceremonial meeting of parliament, I took my oath of office, but I was elected a week before that.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I not remember when you were elected on our joint list?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm just trying to put all the facts together, the facts that I need with regard to these questions, this line of questioning that I've been pursuing. Is it clear that on that day, my term as President of Serbia ceased by virtue of the fact that I was elected President of Yugoslavia and that, therefore, in line with the constitution, it was compulsory to have early presidential elections in Serbia; within two months' time, is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a topic that was included in statements or is this a statement? I don't understand this. Mr. Milosevic seems to be telling me about the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you're here as a witness, not to argue points. This is not a meeting, this is a court hearing. Now, if you can't answer the question, say you can't answer it. Or if you don't understand it, say you don't understand. Yes. What is the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a generally-known fact, therefore, since I assumed the office of President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that according to the constitution, presidential elections had to be held in Serbia within two months' time? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course it was known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know that precisely talks with regard to the estimated number of Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija in that context were quite topical precisely because of the expectation that this time more Albanians would take part in the elections?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question only with yes or no, because it calls for a lengthier answer. If I give a yes or no answer, I can enter a verbal trap that was set by Mr. Milosevic. So I kindly ask the Trial Chamber for instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that the question is quite precise.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said: Is it clear to you then, in view of the coming elections, that it was possible that the discussion on the number of Albanians in Kosovo was topical at that point because of the expectation that Albanians would vote in the elections in larger numbers this time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of Albanians was a topical issue, but the motive why it was so topical is something that requires a lengthier explanation. I kindly ask the Trial Chamber for instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Only a short while ago, you confirmed that at that time, that is to say, in the public, there was a generally-expressed expectation that the process of reintegration of the Kosovo Albanians would start, the reintegration, the political life of Kosovo and -- Serbia and Yugoslavia, and I interrupted you there and you said yes.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course if an agreement is reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please, there was this general expectation, the Milosevic-Rugova agreement had already been signed, the Dayton Peace Accord was already being implemented, tensions were being eased, and in these general expectations that a process of reintegrating the Albanians would start in the political life and then the coming elections for president in view of the fact that my term of office expired. So that had to be held within two months' time. So is it logical to you, because you said it yourself only a short while ago that you could have expected, that there was this general expectation of the political reintegration of Albanians, that forecasts were discussed and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. I'm going to stop this. It's not a question. What you do, Mr. Milosevic, instead of asking questions, you pile assertion upon assertion, and it makes the life of a witness very difficult. He can't answer assertion after assertion. Now, I don't know what the point of all this is. If there is a point, let's get to it. And ask questions more shortly. If you do, we'll get on more quickly and you won't be stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if you take things out of a time context and a political context, they look different. And if you put them in a time context and political context, then they are clear, and then they are -- they can be explained. And I imagine that this is quite clear to you as to an intellectual. So the witness confirmed that at that time in mid 1997, there was a general expectation that the process of reintegration of the Albanians would start.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not confirm that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. For a moment. You've been over this. You are asking questions. You are not engaging in an argument with this witness. Now, the way to put a question is to put it shortly and go from point to point. That's the way to conduct the examination, rather than a series of assertions, which is quite impossible for the witness to answer. Now, we've spent a very long time on this particular point, and I still am not following what it is that you are putting to the witness. Can you put a series of short questions? And it may be then we can move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of such an atmosphere, which I hope you understand the way I explained it to you, was there an expectation that this time Albanians would vote in the coming presidential elections in greater numbers?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We strove for that, that they do vote in the elections and on condition that a political agreement was made, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it logical, then, that when elections are likely and, according to the constitution, will take place within two months' time, that there is a discussion on the number of Albanians that may vote in the election so that this may be taken into account amongst various calculations among persons who are interested in the outcome of these elections, of course? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was logical, that is why we discussed it. Of course. But there was no agreement afterwards. That was the point of what I said. I really do not understand how I'm supposed answer these questions, and I run the risk of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Do you remember the statements made by some of our officials that before the Albanians boycotted the elections, inter alia because they didn't want it to become obvious that there were less of them than they were actually declaring?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, but this is a comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's up to them to decide. A little knowledge is a dangerous thing, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, yes, I cannot answer such equivocal questions. Please could I be instructed on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down for the interpreters. No. Wait a moment. The question was, that you were asked, Mr. Tanic, is this: Do you remember statements made by officials that the Albanians boycotted the elections because they didn't want it to become obvious that there were less of them than they were actually declaring? Now, that was the question. Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were such statements made by Milosevic's associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, do you have an assessment of your own, since you are involved in such things? How many Albanians from Albania are in Kosovo right now, persons who are not citizens of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, for two and a half years now I haven't been involved in politics because we have emigrated, and I have no assessments with regard to the political situation in Kosovo, and I'm not talking about the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that, in Belgrade, the figure 200.000 to 300.000 persons is being mentioned as Albanians who have illegally entered Kosovo from Albania?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not matter for the witness, as he's told you. It's not part of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that only recently in Kosovo and Metohija elections were held that were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- staged by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given an answer to this. He's outside politics and the country. Anyway, it's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He could have read about it in the newspaper that elections were held in Kosovo and Metohija. This is a fact from the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't trouble to answer. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, I advise you, since elections were just held in Kosovo and Metohija now, to have a look at this and see how many Albanians voted in the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we've clarified this: It was expected that Albanians would vote in the elections in larger numbers.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a political agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't go back over old matters. Now, if there's repetition, you'll be stopped. Let us move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Do you know that in Serbia, before elections, as a rule there is no other subject that is discussed apart from elections?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear to you, then, that at that reception that you've been referring to and where discussions were held and where you could have heard - of course, not from me because we never talked - you could have heard how many Albanians there were and that there were less than 1 million of them, that all of this was within the context of the coming elections? Isn't that clear to you at least now?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said, that the number of Albanians was discussed at that reception. It's not that I said that I tortured you in order to disclose a secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, do you remember, since you say that you followed all events very closely, that in that same year, 1997, that is to say it's about two months after that reception where you allegedly talked to me, so do you remember that in that same year, in 1997, in October, a summit meeting was held, a meeting of heads of state or government of south-eastern Europe, in Crete?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that it was devoted to regional integration and cooperation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the major step that was made towards the normalisation of relations between Yugoslavia and Albania when Fatos Nano, the then-Prime Minister of Albania and I, before the TV cameras, said that we are starting normalisation, the opening of borders, that we will abolish visas, that we will develope trade and tourism, et cetera, et cetera. Do you remember that? That was carried by all televisions.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that I remember that but I was one of the people who commented on the development of relations between Yugoslavia and Albania in your newspaper Politika.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember, then, that Fatos Nano then stated that the relations with Kosovo were an internal affair of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but who is denying that, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point I'm making to you is that throughout that year, until the summit held in Crete, there was a general climate of optimism and also a truly peaceful resolution of all questions in Kosovo and Metohija and in the region, including our relations with Albania. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I said, that there was a political climate and that there was a political agreement that would make it possible to avoid a war, and that is compatible with my claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, if we place this in the context of time and the events that took place, does it become clear how your conclusions are absurd, that is to say that the number -- that the figure of Albanians was to do with ethnic cleansing and not with the forthcoming process of their reintegration into political life, the normalisation of relations and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That does not seem to me to be absurd because the question of the number of Albanians was a subject that was discussed in both contexts and everything was all right until 1998 and until you started with this policy of conflict, engineering that, and that's what I say in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of fact, Mr. Tanic, that this atmosphere of understanding and trust, confidence and optimism that was expressed at the summit on Crete was an alarm signal to the forces which wished to destabilise Yugoslavia and incite terrorism in Kosovo? Is that clear to you? Is that well-known to you as an expert?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but this is a comment and it's not correct at all what Mr. Milosevic just said. It's completely incorrect. I would have to give a lengthy answer. But my answer in fact is that the assertion is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when we saw a breakthrough in the development of relations both in south-eastern Europe and in the Albanian-Yugoslav relations and the calming down of the situation after Dayton, you consider that the figures that were discussed were discussed because of ethnic cleansing and not precisely to further those relations and to bring about integration; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I'm saying. I was just saying that it was the former option of ethnic cleansing. Of course there were honest people who discussed this in the context of elections. It is not true that foreign powers incited terrorism, and I took part in this climate which was improving, and I took part in this and that is why I know and that is why I say that you upset it all in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop -- I'm going to stop you because there must be a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know for sure, is that it, that the foreign services of the foreign powers had no part to play in inciting, financing, organising, training terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija; is that it? You say you know that full well, do you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The foreign powers offered you precisely the opposite, that under conditions of a political agreement, they enable -- they would enable the cutting down of terrorism, Albanian terrorism in Europe, and that is a component part of my statement; and I'm thinking of the Contact Group countries first and foremost in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they did that through you. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only through me, I never said that, I just said that I was one of the people who knew this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who did they do this through? Through whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said this to you directly and in political conversations with your political associates, and I made up an official note about that. I don't wish to raise my own importance, I just want to describe the negative process in which I took part. You have an official note in the archive of the State Security Service, and if there isn't, we'll call in witnesses. You were offered assistance, in the case of a political agreement, assistance to suppress Albanian terrorism. I never defended Albanian terrorism, Mr. Milosevic, I just said that you were overexaggerating the problems and exploiting them, to the detriment of both the Serbs and the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So now you have evolved. You have made a slight step forward, because I asked you whether, under those conditions of a general easing of tensions and normalising of relations, whether it was logical for the figure to be discussed in regard to the elections and not with respect to ethnic cleansing. You said yes in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not going back to this question of the figure and the million. We have spent over half an hour on it. It's quite unnecessary to spend that length of time on the same point. Now, move on to another one, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point is precisely -- the point is precisely, Mr. May, that in this false indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard you make your points. Now, there's no need to continually repeat them. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was saying was that it is the point of this false indictment to accuse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. If you want to continue this cross-examination, you must continue it properly and ask some questions and on a new topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked, I think by Judge Robinson it was, if I remember correctly, but anyway, somebody did ask you, at any rate, where the relevance was. What is the relevance of whether there were more than a million or less than a million? And your answer was that it was because whether they would be treated in a national minority or a constituent people depended on this figure. Am I right in understanding you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the percentages had a great bearing on the understanding and substance of autonomy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know that one of the basic principles of the protection of minority rights and generally the rights of minorities, that they cannot be conditioned by the number of people that belong to a national minority? Are you aware of that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are international rules, but I'm not quite sure that they were respected during your regime, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I should like to ask you not to waste time, our time on your comments. You have made sufficient comment. Would you please answer my questions. Now, where is the status of the Albanians different - of whom there are a million - from the status of the Hungarians, for example, or the Bulgarians, or the Ruthenians, or the Slovaks or any other national minority, not to enumerate all of them now, in Serbia? Where is the difference? What was -- how was their status different?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a minority numbers 100.000 or 200.000 people, it cannot have the same status as people that number 1 million in a country of 7 million. Otherwise, I'm not quite clear on your question because Kosovo already had territorial autonomy, and I don't understand where the problem was with this autonomy for Kosovo as you raised it, except for showing that the Albanians were not the majority there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've gone too far. The Albanians were undoubtedly the majority population in Kosovo. Nobody ever questioned that. But you've gone too far. I asked you where the difference in status was, and you said of course there was a difference in status. Of course it's different if the national minority numbers 100.000 and another that numbers 1 million; and that is quite the reverse, it is quite the opposite. Are you aware that that is quite opposite and contrary to the general principles and rights of minorities? That they cannot be conditioned by their numbers and that if somebody belongs to a national minority which has 1 million, that they have greater rights than others who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is going to bring this part of the cross-examination to a close. We have now spent much too long on this particular point of numbers. We have exhausted the topic. If you want to continue this cross-examination, you must go on to another area, Mr. Milosevic. There are a great many areas in this witness's evidence, and you know that your time is limited. You should move on to something else now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's why I said that I would need more time, because the witness explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're wasting time with this. Now, let us move on to another area of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked a question. I asked the same question that one of you gentlemen posed, that is to say where the relevance lies of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over the point now several times. Now, let us move on. We do not wish to hear anything more about numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it clear to you that in the evidence as to the negotiations that the other side provided us with, that you have shown and demonstrated precisely the opposite, the contrary, that we can't speak about any negotiations here, and your party, that is something that your party states in quite precise terms. The policy that you presented us with - I don't want to waste time and read it all - but this scientific symposium, it says, which has political implications was attended by you, et cetera, et cetera, then Simic and the rest, a scientific symposium.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which has political implications as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, political implications. Mr. Tanic, every scientific symposium dealing with a political topic must have political implications. That's quite clear to one and all, it's just very logical. Now, in view of the fact that you have not completed your schooling, how did you manage to take part in a scientific symposium? What science do you delve in?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question -- first of all, I didn't say that I have not completed my schooling. You tested the level of my university training. I said that it was a private question and that I didn't want to answer and that was a rude question on your part. But I took part in a political capacity and not a scientific capacity at the meeting. I never claimed that I was a scientist or scientific worker, and that was my function there. And it was published in the papers as well. I never represented myself as being a scientist, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this piece of evidence - it is an article in the newspaper Politika - which says that this was a scientific symposium and, in the title, it says, "A Scientific Symposium Held Recently in Munich." That is the main title. And you represented that falsely as being negotiations.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to ask the Trial Chamber, please, I never misrepresented this as negotiations. I put forward documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is correct. We have the exhibit in front of us. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not that you represented this as being negotiations, not only that, but you represented them to be as negotiations that you took part in, following my own authorisation.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I represented this to be a component part of the negotiating process. I always spoke of a process, the process was ongoing for three years. It had several tens or dozens of component parts. Some of them were in the form of symposiums, other ones were tete-a-tete negotiations. It was a process, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this symposium in Munich, you considered that to be part of the negotiating process; is that it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of the links of this negotiating process which went on for three weeks [as interpreted]. It was a scientific discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if it was a negotiating process, that means that you considered it to be negotiations, in fact.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Is that a statement or are you asking me a question? I said clearly that it was part of the negotiating process which had many parts and lasted for over three years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say that this scientific symposium was part of the negotiating process. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In conformity with your desire to have NGO groups, scientific institutions, professional institutions take part to discuss the problem from various aspects and dimensions, and of course, your instructions were adhered to both by domestic factors and foreign factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean I gave instructions to go to Munich to have a scientific symposium held there? Was that my instruction? Is that what you're saying? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specific instructions for Munich. What you called for was that, instead of the state organs, we have preparations for the Kosovo negotiations by non-governmental organisations, notable ones, so that we could avoid having people say that a third party was being involved in Yugoslavia's internal affairs. You expressed that desire not only in my presence or Mr. Mihajlovic's presence, but you said that in front of foreign ambassadors and we'll call them to testify here as witnesses. Your wishes were respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, please, my stance and positions can be read about in the papers. You needn't seem to be discovering some common standpoints and positions that I personally stated and were published in the press that anybody could read in the papers or see on television. There's nothing to prove there. Well, I doubt that they could all see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Just one moment. Now, this is not an argument. This is supposed to be a cross-examination from which we will gain assistance. And at the moment, it seems to be an argument. Mr. Milosevic, would you concentrate on asking questions shortly and to the point, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that the questions are very concise and short, but I'll try and be briefer still.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these joint recommendations on the Kosovo conflict, that you participants compiled them, Bertelsmann and so on and so forth, the scientific centre, et cetera, and that the Germans and the French adopted those recommendations, that paper; is that right? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't ask -- you can't answer all questions with a yes or no so that I fall into your verbal trap. The activities of the NGO and the Bertelsmann Foundation went on for two years, and yes, at the -- in the end, the paper was adopted which expressed the spirit of what was discussed, and later on, the substance of that document became an initiative on the part of the German and French diplomacy and later on by the European Union. Not word-for-word but the substance of the document, that is to say, the step-by-step approach, the three-stage development, a provisional political agreement, and so on and so forth. And that's why I presented that document, to show the spirit and stand of European diplomacy and contact groups.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, could you explain to Mr. Tanic that he would have to be concrete and brief in his answers and that they must be answers in response to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was nothing wrong with that answer. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, the Germans and the French adopted the recommendations which they ordered to have compiled themselves; is that it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the Germans and the French but German and French diplomacy, later the diplomacy of the European Union and not ones that they had ordered themselves but negotiations with the Serbs, the Albanians and the representatives of the international community all took part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about somebody in the name of the Serbian government? Did they represent -- did they take part, people who represented official Serb positions, or was that you? Did you ascribe that function to you yourself?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to facilitate the work of the court, whether I ascribe something to myself or not, let me leave that aside. But the Bertelsmann Foundation worked in close cooperation with Monsignor Paglia and your personal associates, Mr. Ratko Markovic and Mr. Dojcilo Maslovaric, had contacts with them. Let us forget myself because I say that I can always testify to circumstances that can be proved from two or three aspects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you whether at these preparations that you say went on for two years were participated in by any official representatives of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they take part?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, first and foremost, this was a process in which several NGOs took part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you when. Don't make speeches to me that this was a process, et cetera, et cetera. When?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting from the first meeting that was held, the one that was organised by Ambassador Roberts in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a reception of Mr. Roberts'?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, it was a meeting at Sava Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again a round-table discussion.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. It was a conference, it was called a round-table conference, but why are we engaging in such a verbal traps again? Now Mr. Milosevic is making me decide between two very unfavourable options; I should either be impolite or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't comment. Don't comment. Mr. Tanic, if you feel you can't answer the question, simply say, "I can't answer that," or something of the sort. Now, Mr. Milosevic, will you bear in mind that the interpreters have to interpret this. So will you leave a gap after the answer before you ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just stress that. I don't know whether the accused and the witness appreciate the need for the pause. In the vast majority of cases, we have a witness speaking in one language and the examiner speaking in a different language so that, ordinarily, the pause is there, but in a case where the witness and the examiner use the same language, there is a tendency to overlap. In many instances, because you are speaking the same language, you quite often even begin an answer before the question is completed, and I can sense that the interpreters are having a very, very difficult time with the interpretation of the exchanges between the witness and the accused. So I must stress the importance of a pause. Resist the temptation to rush into an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in these joint recommendations, it says that the Albanians should have the right to use their own language in the process of education, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I do not understand the point of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what the joint recommendations say?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. This is a general matter. This was not the core of these recommendations. The core was that there would be three stages involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer my question. How can someone then who comes from Serbia, who doesn't even have to represent the government, how can someone write that when this was never denied and when, according to our laws, the Albanian language was equal to the Serbian language in Kosovo? How can that be recommended? How can I recommend it to you to shave your head when you haven't shaved your head? How --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can I recommend something that is so obvious?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put a short question to the witness so he can understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the recommendation is to use the Albanian language in Kosovo and Metohija and the Albanian language is, was, and remained in use as the official language in Kosovo, equal to the Serbian language, how can a recommendation be made to achieve something that has already been achieved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow that question because it's another speech. Yes. The next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This third document that you also presented and that you claim is a joint effort, et cetera, et cetera, it's called "Exploring Futures for Kosovo, Kosovo Albanians and Serbs in Dialogue, Project Report." That's what I got, in this form. I'm not going to quote anything from there. I don't want to waste time. But half of the papers that are contained in this document -- four papers, as a matter of fact, and there are four more, I didn't even look at them. What the foreigners or -- well, anyway, there is one, "Kosovo Republic in a New Confederation via Federalisation of Yugoslavia," Jasmin Pulja [phoen]. That is one of the titles. "The Autonomy Statute of Trentino South Tyrol, European Model for the Kosovo Crisis," Predrag Simic [phoen]. "Draft Principles for the Sovereign State of the Republic of Kosovo," Esad Simic [phoen]. "How to realise independence for Kosovo," Martin Brosis [phoen]. Is it clear that half of these papers call for the independence of Kosovo and a Republic of Kosovo as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the tasks of scientific gatherings is to look at different contexts from the worst case scenario to the best case scenario in order to avert further danger on the ground. That is why all options were covered, that is to say from autonomy to the independence of Kosovo so that it would be easier both for the Serb and the Albanian side and there would be less problems on the ground. Nobody asked for anything there. I describe the spirit of the process and I'm saying that there was a political process, nothing else, and that it was favourable to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. A process in question there are seven or eight of you, and then papers are presented on the independence of Kosovo and you believe that that is a political process which resolves problems. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, you did not understand me correctly. I presented this only as part of a total where my own paper's included and I say that this was an authorised approach by the Serb side. You authorised it, step-by-step in three stages, no independence whatsoever, but this is put in a scientific way. And there were people there who wanted to test the negative scenarios as well, precisely to help the authorities in Belgrade in order to avoid this. It's not that somebody was looking for something. I presented this only because of my own paper, because of my own platform, because I don't have any other papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, this is the first time I hear that you have a platform of your own.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying it's a platform of my own, I just presented this in order to show what I was defending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it's time for an adjournment. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a little while ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I haven't objected to any of the questions this morning because I have no doubt my objection would have added to the difficulties the Court is encountering, but I would urge that the Court consider abbreviating the cross-examination unless it's going to become more useful, but that's matter entirely for the Court. If the Court is going to allow the accused to go beyond today, I shan't be here on Tuesday, and I would invite the Court to require him to deal with examination on any security issues today, simply because they are matters about which I am much better informed than any others, and they're not necessarily matters that are widely-known amongst our team. So it would be preferable if he could deal with those today. Preferable, so far as I'm concerned, that he should finish altogether today, but that's a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you say "security issues," these are the issues concerned with what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Communication with intelligence agencies and matters of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I advised Mr. Nice during the break that there would be one or two issues in relation to that matter that I would be touching upon in questioning this particular witness which will go to issues of credibility. It won't be extensive, but it would be of a limited form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we shall have to decide what, if any, time the accused should have on Tuesday morning. Meanwhile, Mr. Milosevic, if you can deal with those issues. You've heard what counsel has said and if you can deal with them, you should today. But we have a more general announcement to make because during the adjournment, we have taken the opportunity of considering the conduct of the cross-examination so far. We are of the view that far too much time has been wasted in repetition and personal argument between the witness and the accused.
